Thank you. I'm here. Okay, great. So distinguished panelists and guests, thank you so much for having CALP here. The GHA report tells us what we already feel: humanitarian funding is Falling and the gap between need and resources is widening. But unlike— but alongside the funding crisis, there is an efficiency crisis. And unlike the funding crisis, this one is largely in our power to fix. So the question is not only how we mobilize more diverse and predictable resources, but it's also how we use evidence to make resources we have already more flexible effective and accountable. So I'm going to draw on 3 points, and that is better prioritization, stronger accountability, and better delivery. And all 3 of these evidence points in the same direction and are connected to cash assistance. [FOREIGN LANGUAGE] So first, finance what delivers the greatest impact per dollar. Recent research from the CaLP Network found that multi-purpose cash assistance is up to 36% 27.5% more cost-efficient than in-kind food assistance. So, at a global scale, this translates into $1 to $3 billion US that could be used more effectively every year, enough to reach 60 million more people without raising a single additional dollar. Now, that last number should really give us pause.
Absolutely.

Because it means every year we don't make this shift, We are leaving 60 million people unserved. Cash assistance is also the most flexible modality, easy for the system to scale up and easy to scale down, and it is flexible for the people who receive it. Second, use data from crisis-affected people to guide resource allocation. New findings that we're finalizing in a report that will be out in September shows that when people affected by crisis are asked asked how they want to receive assistance, guess what they say? In Afghanistan, 89% said cash. In Myanmar, between 90% and 98% said cash, and in Ukraine, 79%. So these are not marginal preferences. They reflect something fundamental. People want agency, the ability to decide for their own households, not to have decisions made for them. Thank you.. And people-centered humanitarian system takes that seriously. Yet financing decisions do not always reflect this evidence. And the recent UNHCR report shows that cash and voucher assistance— Juliette pointed out— still holding its own, just about 20% of the total IHA. But if we're serious about flexible financing, then donor allocations and funding instruments should be designed to respond to evidence from affected communities. And not assumptions about what people need. And my third point is— and it speaks to what Malini was talking about— see local actors as part of the financing solution. [SPEAKING IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE] And this is about who delivers cash assistance, and it has direct implications on localization. So the conversation of localization is often framed as a question of equity and participation, which are really important reasons. But the evidence points also to a financing rationale. Our data, admittedly a small sample because local actors receive only a tiny share of direct funding, but it shows that local organizations delivering cash assistance achieve 73% cost efficiency, meaning nearly three-quarters of every dollar reaches a person in crisis. So these are not marginal actors. They are often the most efficient, and the most trusted that we have, with a proximity and contextual knowledge that is hard to replicate from outside. And in a world of shrinking resources, investing directly in capable local actors implementing cash assistance is not only the right thing to do, it's how we stretch funding further. [FOREIGN LANGUAGE] So here's where I'm landing. Choosing the most efficient modality makes resources more flexible, anchoring decisions in what affected people tells us makes them more accountable. And channeling more of the money through local actors makes the system more diverse and responsive. And all of this points to cash assistance. Now, none of this requires new money. It requires using what we already have, but using it differently. And we're in a moment of constrained resources and hard choices. And this panel is exactly the right place to ask, are we making those choices based on evidence? Because evidence is clear. Cash assistance is more efficient, it's no riskier, it's what people want, and local actors can deliver it effectively. So what we need now is decision-making by donors, governments, coordinators, and operational actors that systematically reflects what evidence tells us. In a constrained environment, Evidence is not simply a tool for accountability, it is one of our most important tools for improving how the humanitarian system prioritizes, finances, and delivers assistance. Thank you.

We are seeing the retrenchment and unfortunately the retreat of many donors. And with that undeniable and ruthless prioritization that really focuses on the lifesaving assistance, which we all completely agree is necessary, too often comes at the expense or is forced to compete with the underlying resilience and anticipatory action activities that we have all seen is what actually reduces the cure on the backend. Our oft-quoted piece in our organization is, "An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure." And while that may be trite, it really has been borne out both from a financial perspective and from an infrastructure, sweat equity, and engagement perspective. This takes the grinding, hard-boring, unsexy engagement of humanitarians as well as policymakers and ensuring that the evidence that we have is turned into action, that we are creative in our communication and persistent in our engagement while still maintaining the IHL principles and our core tenets, in hopefully more creative ways and engaging ways as we have to meet this moment. We are making a very clear, conscious choice to continue to support the existing principled multilateral approach to humanitarian aid. We still very much believe in that system. We think it is a good system. But we're also brutally clear, and we want to be brutally clear with everybody, that it's a system that needs to be reformed, and we need to become much more effective in how we deliver and how we work. A big part of that for us is around collaboration and dealing with the fragmentation that you currently see in the system. I think you raised the question, Juliette, earlier in, in one of your slides, of of what happens to those who are not prioritized, and I fully recognize that that is a legitimate question, it's a fair question. But I think the more fundamental question at this moment in time is how do we serve more people with the money we have and try to become more effective and efficient and cost-efficient with the funding that is available so that we enlarge the group of people that can be served and reduce that second group of people that is currently not targeted. I really would plead to put the effectiveness and efficiency question up front in all of the thinking on this. I have mentioned this in every meeting I've been in so far, but I will mention it again: supply chain, humanitarian supply chains. I mean, we're talking about 60 to 70% of the cost of humanitarian aid today. It cannot be the right approach that everybody just works on their own. This needs to be consolidated. It needs to be fully, fully integrated, and we very much recognize the ongoing work that's taking place on this, but it needs to be accelerated and it needs to be scaled up.

Cash.

We very much believe in cash. We are fully with you, Holly. Multipurpose cash is the best approach wherever local economies can sustain it. And that is also not to be taken for granted, because I've also been in places where beneficiaries actually told me, "I don't want the cash." I mean, it also— these places also exist. I mean, some in South Sudan, some parts of the country cannot sustain cash at this moment in time. But wherever it is possible, this should be the default mode, and this is the approach that we are absolutely favoring and prioritizing in all of our funding. I don't think the resistance to cash comes from donors necessarily. I think sometimes it comes from implementing partners. And I think we're certainly with you, and we're very happy to work work with all of the partners to be more efficient on this. When Holly says that— and I believe you, Holly— that cash assistance is 37.5% more efficient than food aid in kind, well, then that's a statistic we can simply not ignore. And that goes back to this question of how do we serve more people with the funding that today is available. Marlene, I hear you loud and clear, and I'm fully with you. Localization, it is— it's difficult, but it is incredibly important, and it is an area where collectively we all need to do better for all the reasons that you and others have mentioned. So, I don't need to repeat those reasons and the benefits. I think the difficulty is in the financing models, and I'll be very open and transparent with you. In the EU today, it is legally impossible for me to fund local organizations directly. Is that going to change? I don't think so, because with all of the— all of the scrutiny we have from auditors, from taxpayers, And from everybody. It is not going to go in that direction anytime soon. We also need to be honest and clear about that. However, we are committing very clearly that we will, as of next year, we will spend a minimum of 25% of all of our humanitarian funding as directly as possible to local actors. And in some countries, we're far beyond that. 20%. In Ukraine, we are far above 25%. In other countries, it is more difficult, but the direction of travel is very clear. We're also stepping up our contributions to the country-based pooled funds, not as radically as some others are, but we are stepping up and we're also taking that very seriously. And we think it is the right way to go, and there, there's real work for you, Enrique, to make sure that the country-based pooled funds favour that localization and really create space for that localization. We need to be smarter, as was said, about how we work on this, and you spoke about anticipatory action, and there I also fully agree. There's one really cool project we're doing with with the World Food Programme that I want to mention in one sentence. In the Middle East, which currently today is a region that is in complete turmoil, and which is very important for us as the European Union, for a long time we've been running emergency after emergency, sort of, and we're now trying to change that. And we've set up a trust fund together, I mean, or WFP has set up a fund that will allow them to preposition food stocks and replenish food stocks very clearly whenever something else happens in that region, so that we can react much more quickly, we can anticipate developments and react more quickly when needed. We're doing lots of anticipatory action in the Americas for the hurricane season, for the cyclone season. We know when it's coming, we know how it needs to be responded under to. two, and I think this needs to be rolled out much more broadly. Data— none of these approaches are possible without credible, good data. We need reliable data. We need the UN system and the humanitarian system at large to become much better at data and much more joined up, less fragmented. I also want to pick up on two or three points that were mentioned briefly only, but leadership. This is about collaboration and it is about leadership, and I think what we need to keep firmly in mind, and I'm looking again in the direction of Ocha here, is that the real test for the reset is the ability of— or is your ability to bring the others on board and to make sure that the whole humanitarian community rallies behind the reset, and I would really encourage you to spend time on that. I mean, it is not going to work unless everybody owns the reset, and we as donors will do our part in that. We will encourage, we will incentivize, and we will punish eventually if it doesn't work. But I think it is really something we want to emphasize. So we need to see OCHA leadership in all of this. We need to see local leadership for the humanitarian and resident coordinators. We need to have the right people in place who can think broadly, who can think across the different sort of instruments and agencies. Fundamentally, this is also about the role of humanitarian aid in protracted crisis. We keep using the smallest budget —of all budgets—to try and solve very long, very large crises. In countries—I'm not going to name countries—but in some countries, we are using the international humanitarian aid budget to provide basic services to the population because governments are failing to do so and because development actors are pulling out. That's wrong. That is plainly wrong. And that means that we cannot use that humanitarian aid funding to serve people in other places in urgent need. And so we need to find— we need to work really on that self-reliance dimension. We need to deal with aid dependency and try and promote self-reliance, try and promote economic opportunities for beneficiaries, and try to be very honest, as you said, Hendrika, about the limitations of the humanitarian aid system, and I think we're not doing that enough. And just to finish off, we need more diverse funding sources—philanthropy, the international financial institutions—we need to bring all of those more on board, but most importantly, we need to reduce the needs for humanitarian aid, and that means working on IHL, it means working on ensuring respect for basic rules in armed conflict, it means ensuring respect for humanitarian access, and there, collectively, we all need to step up big time. Thank you so much.

Thank you very, very much, sir. And I want to thank everybody else for your attendance today. I wish you a very productive remainder of 2026 ECOSOC Humanitarian Affairs Segment. And with those remarks, this meeting is now closed. Thank you.
